"Let that give you no concern, sir," answered Gormly; "I pray that you consider the place and all in it as your own. I beg you take off your wraps and make yourselves entirely at home."

"That's very handsome of you, I am sure," continued the elder Haldane, slowly removing his coat; "but my own place lies but six miles beyond here, and if you will permit us to telephone my stables, I think we shall have to trouble you but little."

his fingers upon his palm.
"Done what?" asked Miss Burton, giving a nervous start.

"Made you forget your dignity and all
that, and come right out and talk things

you think that I would not be willing to
come right out and talk things over with
you?"

"You did. You came into this room
this evening and looked down on me and
said to yourself: Young man, it is my
duty to prove to you, in as few words
possible, that you are not welcome—and
think I shall enjoy putting you back in
your proper element as quickly and firm
ly as possible. That is what you
thought, but I wanted to take you out of
yourself first, so that we'd have a fair
start. Now I am ready for the verdict."

Miss Burton looked down at the floor.
The shaded lamps threw a soft light over
her, and it suddenly occurred to Dick
that she was not at all bad looking. Miss
Burton was one of those women who,
having once yielded to their relatives in
a matter of moment, devote the balance
of their lives silently to holding up this
compliance as the cause of all subsequent
unhappiness, no matter how remote it
may be. And for fear that the unhap-
piness would not be sufficiently conspicu-
ous, develop an expression of martyrlike
submission, which serves a perennial
accusation against these unhappy and re-
pentant relatives.

Even as the intoxicated man is seldom
so far under the influence of drink that
some part of his personality is not aware
of his irrational acts, so Miss Burton
fully understood that her attitude was a
species of torture to those about her.
Yet, having deliberately chosen this plan,
consciousness of it only served to in-
struct her in bringing it to a higher state
of perfection.

But so artificial a warping of human
beauty could not endure the strong rays
from Dick's normal personality, and when
Miss Burton let her eyes fall to the floor,
all the wasted years of her narrow life

seemed to crowd about her to clamor at
the starvation with which she had fed
them. She could not understand her
feelings; it was nothing he had said. It
was not even himself as an individual.

It was the spirit of youth which she had
denied, and which had returned when
least expected to taunt and disarm her.
"Let's go out into the moonlight," sug-
gested Dick, after a minute's silence.

"The night is beautiful and no matter
what you have to say, it will be easier to
say it in the moonlight."

His voice had grown serious at the
thought of all this message might mean
to him, for the continued absence of Kate
convinced him that the decision had not
been in his favor.

"Katherine's father insisted on her ac-
companying him to New York to do some
shopping and plan some recreation for
the evening," explained Miss Burton.
She did not know that she was going
to say it, and afterward she did not
know why she had said it, but when
Dick said, "Thank you," very softly, she
was surprised to see how glad she was
that she had said it.

"Well, shall we go outdoors?" he asked
again. "It is criminal to stay in the
house such a night as this."

"Yes, I think it would be very enjoy-
able in the moonlight," replied Miss Bur-
ton, a little wistfully. "I shall get a
wrap at once."

"I am going bareheaded," announced
the primitive Richard.

"Then I am going bareheaded, too,"
said the sedate Miss Burton, with a
laugh, which differed materially from any
which had passed her lips for years.
She picked up a white knitted scarf as
they passed through the hall, and soon
they were together in the shadows of the
trees. It seemed like a dream to her; for
so many years she had developed an af-
fection that it had become reality to
herself and all about her; and now the
youth, her own youth, which she had im-
prisoned long ago, had returned, laugh-
ing coyly, thrilling with exhilaration at
what was really an adventure, and won-
derful with the reincarnation of that free
girlish shyness which is a mixture of
challenge, inexperience and the secretive-
ness of the wild thing which watches the
hunter from a thicket and half hopes for
discovery and the glorious chase after-
ward with its own life as the prize.

And Dick was not playing a part either:
at least not purposely playing one. Miss
Burton was an original character, pos-
sessing an individuality which interested
him, and it always afforded him wealth
of amusement to rout old age and make
old folk feel and act like children. He
invariably made companions of those
about him, age, sex nor species being
allowed to interfere.

A stretch of smooth sward, flecked with
moonlight, spread out before them. "I
can beat you to that big oak tree," cried
Dick, pointing.

She looked into his face a moment and
then without a word turned and ran with
surprising lightness toward the tree. Dick
followed, drew alongside and made the
race a tie.

"Dear, dear," she said, catching her
breath. "I haven't run that far for years; it
must be twenty years."

Her face was flushed, her eyes danced
and as Dick noted them with the critical
eye of a connoisseur, it occurred to him
that twenty years ago he would have
been sorely tempted to claim a prize at
the end of the race.

"You don't look much older than that
yourself," was what he said. "I'll tell
you what I'd like to do, I'd like to put
tick-tack on somebody's window. Are
you game?"

"Not that game," replied Miss Burton,
laughing—it was so easy to laugh this
evening. "I never could stand another
run, and I am sure we'd be chased if you
were the leader."

"Well, come along, then, and we'll see if
there is any mischief to get into on these
grounds; and as we walk I'll tell you
something funny. For several days I
thought my uncle wanted me to marry
you—and I was already head over heels
in love with your niece."

"Marry me?" exclaimed Miss Burton,
almost recovering her dignity.

"Yes, you see it was this way," and
Dick swung into a full account of all that
had taken place since his return.

"It certainly is lots of fun to be young,"
she said, with a sigh, when at last he had
finished.

"Yes, and the best of it is that it is the
privilege of all free people," added Dick. "Only
the slaves of the years get old.
Now for instance, here is a swing," he
said, pointing to one which had been
erected to entertain the Sunday school
class which a friend of Kate's taught,
and which had been allowed to remain.
"Old folk would pass this swing grunting
and grumbling, but we shall get in and
take a ride."

"Oh, no, there is a limit to my folly,"
protested Miss Burton; but all the time
she was being led toward the swing, and
soon she was seated in it, and Dick was
pushing vigorously until the ropes
creaked and Miss Burton, with little gasps
and whoops, found herself soaring in.

known for several years, and we had two
or three drinks together and the con-
versation drifted to cotton. I expressed a
belief that cotton would decline 100 points

The completion of this work was celebrated in fine style today. The largest crowd in the history of Wingate assembled here today. It seemed that not only all Union county came, but many from Mecklenburg and Anson, and South Carolina counties came also.

The principal address was made by Governor W. W. Kitchin. When he arose to speak at noon today, standing on the porch of the old building of the school, the main auditorium was packed and people, as far as could hear, were standing on all sides. The Governor made a great educational speech, touching not a word on the senatorial campaign.

For weeks and weeks the trustees, friends and officers of the Wingate school, a preparatory school of this section, have watched for the day when the corner stone was to be laid. That day is now history.

Today the corner stone of the new building was laid by the Masonic Lodge. Mr. J. W. Rowell, Masonic lecturer, represented the Grand Master, Mr. R. S. Hackett, who was unable to be present. Mr. R. H. Bradley, of Raleigh, assisted in the work.

Directly following the laying of the corner stone the crowd assembled in front of the old school building auditorium to hear Governor Kitchin. The people were welcomed by Mr. J. W. Powell and Rev. D. M. Austin introduced the speaker, Governor W. Kitchin. Governor Kitchin spoke about an hour and aside from the remarks of the introductory speaker, no one would have known that he was a candidate for any office. He mentioned nothing at all politically. Governor Kitchin took as his subject, "Education," and made a good address. He said that a good citizen must be educated, to make him a more intelligent voter.

Good citizenship, said the Governor, is composed of three qualities, intelligence, morality, courage.

In speaking of why a good citizen needs courage, he said, "I've been your governor for two and one-half years, and I have been your governor, too, although I have not had quite as much help as some others.

Have friends, said the Governor, be friendly to all. I don't say, have no enemies, for as long as there is sin and corruption, and some one is profiting by them, those that try to put down corruption and sin will always have enemies. Men will do all manner of things against you, they will try to make the public think you are hypocrites and scoundrels.

Be friendly to all," he said. "I try to do that. I try to have a brotherly feeling, and build up rather than tear down. I have devoted my time to you and for you good. I am not perfect and I have not seen one recently who is." He thanked the crowd for their rapt attention and sat down without mentioning politics or the senatorship. He is meeting the people today and making friends of them all.

The crowd was at 1000. Everything was quiet and the day passed off orderly.

Never before and probably never again will Wingate have such a day.

time, the world's uplifting period, the
regeneration epoch for mankind, shall
not begin until first the true Church,
the "little flock," the Bride of Christ,
shall be completed and be united or
married to the Heavenly Bridegroom
beyond the veil—made partaker with
Him of glory, honor and immortality,
the divine nature.

Plan of the Ages, timed by Infinite
Wisdom, has delayed long enough to
permit you and me and all of God's
Spirit-begotten children to make our
calling and our election sure to a
share with our Redeemer in His
glorious work. How glad we are that
the door of opportunity to this high
calling still stands open and that the
Heavenly Father and the Kingly Re-
deemer are reckoning us to share the
things which eye hath not seen nor
ear heard, neither have entered into
the heart of man, but which are re-
served for us and for all who love
Him sincerely—more than they love
houses or lands, parents or children
or self.

Washington, May 30.—That the government means to formulate its antitrust policies in accordance with the rule of reason as laid down by the Supreme Court in the Standard Oil and Tobacco trust decisions, notwithstanding the vigorous dissents of Associate Justice Harlan, and the large number of bills introduced in the Senate to amend the Sherman antitrust law was made evident today.

Administration officials, after a day's consideration and study of the tobacco decision and a thorough comparison with the Standard Oil decision, were agreed that the Rule of reason is no new feature of the Supreme Court's interpretation of law and one member of the cabinet, whose views have always been regarded as rejecting those of the administration, made a comprehensive statement to that effect.

The statement was attributed to an official close to the administration. It follows in part:

Justice Harlan, in his dissenting opinion in the Tobacco case, objects vigorously to the application in the construction of the act of Congress of the Rule of reason to which attention was called by the Chief Justice in his opinion in the Standard Oil case and again in the Tobacco case. Justice Harlan declares that to insert by construction the words "reasonable" or "undue" in the Sherman act is judicial legislation. Congress, he says, has in language so clear and simple that there is no room whatever for construction, signified its purpose to forbid restraint of trade in whatever form, to whatever extent, whereas the court under the Chief Justice's opinion inserts in the law words which make Congress say that it means only to prohibit "undue restraint of trade." This he objects to as amounting to a reading into the act by judicial legislation of an exception not placed there by the law-making branch of the government, and this he contends, the court cannot, and ought not to do.

But Justice Harlan has not always regarded the judicial function as excluding the right to interpret statutes and a liberal construction and wise literal application to the words of the act where that would involve a manifest wrong. In the case of Church of the Holy Trinity against United States, the court had under consideration the act of Congress known as the alien immigration law in 1885.

The Church of the Holy Trinity in New York had made a contract with Rev. Walpole Warren, an alien, residing in England, to remove to New York and into its service as its rector and pastor for a compensation to be paid him; and because of that contract, an action was brought against the church by the United States to recover the penalty prescribed for a violation of this act. Justice Brewer wrote the opinion of the court, in which all the other justices, including Justice Harlan, concurred. He proceeded by conceding that the act of the corporation is within the letter of this section, for the relation of rector to his church is one of service and implies labor on the one side with compensation on the other.

He further noted that certain specific exceptions made in the act in which clergymen were not included strengthened the idea that every other kind of labor and service was intended to be reached by the statute. Yet notwithstanding all of that, it was said that the court could not think that Congress intended to denounce the penalties of a transaction like the employment of a Christian minister.

It is a familiar rule, said Justice Brewer, that a thing may be within the letter of the statute and yet not within the statute, because not within its spirit nor within the intention of its makers. This has been often asserted and the reports are full of cases illustrating its application. This is not the substitution of the will of the judge for that of the legislator, for frequently words of general meaning are used in statute, words broad enough to include an act in question, and yet a consideration of the whole legislation, or of the circumstances surrounding its enactment, or of the absurd results which follow from giving such broad meaning to the words, makes it unreasonable to believe that the legislator intended to include the particular act. by former Senator Beveridge, and all the
Beveridge adherents in the state, includ-
ing majority of the state committee and
the legislature, have stood by Lee, who is
admitted by the regular republicans to be
a man of ability and tact. The old-line
republicans have objected to Lee's ap-
pointment as marshal because it would
have the effect of giving federal recogni-
tion to the Beveridge wing of the party.

They have not centered upon anybody
to present against Lee, but have made
numerous suggestions. The President at
offering Lee position in Washington,
preferably an authorship, but Mr. Lee
declined this, saying he does not wish to
come to Washington to live.

Beveridge two nights ago the President
indicated clearly that he did not deem it
advisable to make Mr. Lee marshal and
that he was hoping to get Mr. Moores
to accept the position. Determined to
have Mr. Lee placed in a good federal
berth in Indiana, Senator Beveridge in-
quired if the President would name the
state chairman as collector of internal
revenue if there should be a vacancy in
the position. The President is said to have expressed his willingness to do this. Mr. Beveridge
is now seeking to have one of his friends,
Elan Neal, retire as collector of internal
revenue so that the position may go to
Lee. Neal was appointed upon the recon-
mendation of Mr. Beveridge, who would
naturally prefer to hold both the mar-
shalship and collectorship for his friends.
Ex-senator Hemenway of Indiana and
Representative Crumpacker of the same
state, both opposed to the appointment
of Lee as marshal, conferred with the
President today about the patronage sit-
uation.

Mr. Moores has not been identified with
either of the factions in Indiana in a
prominent way, although he is said to
have sympathized with the old-line peo-
ple, who will make no objection to him.

The Montana Marshalship.

Senator Dixon of Montana, who clashed
with former Senator Carter a
few months ago over the United States
marshalship of that state, visited the
President today. Mr. Carter, whose term
as senator expired March last, induced
the President to name Charles S. Hem-
derson of Butte as marshal. Mr. Dixon
would not let the nomination be con-
firmed, and now seeks to name a man of
his own for marshal. This will have to
be settled soon.

J. C. Napier, the new register of the
Treasury, called on the President today
with Assistant Register Adams and
Whitefield McKinlay, collector of the port
of Georgetown, to thank him for Napier's
appointment, and to express to him the
appreciation of the negro race for his
splendid letter of confidence to and in
Booker Washington, printed from New
York yesterday. The President told the
visitors, they said, that he always be-
lieved in standing by a real man when
in trouble.

Cecil Lyon, republican national com-
mitteeman of Texas, and Newell Sanders,
republican national committeeman of
Tennessee talked with the President.

Kurt Gosiich, reserve lieutenant in
the German army, and prominent in the
business world of Berlin, paid his re-
spects to the President. He was cordial-
ly received.

Judgeship Vacancy in Massachusetts

Eugene P. Carver of Boston discussed
with the President today the vacancy in
the United States circuit court of Mas-
sachusetts, caused by the death of Judge
Francis C. Lowell. Mr. Carver was in-
troduced to the President by Representa-
tive Weeks. Mr. Carver said that the
majority of the lawyers and judges in
the state preferred to see Judge Fred-
erick Dodge of the United States district
court. There are forty or fifty candidates for the va-
cancy.

Delegates Cameron and Andrews of
Arizona and New Mexico, respectively, called on the
President, who addressed them as "the senators from Arizona
and New Mexico."

President Taft was today invited to
attend the great international dinner
of the Aeronautical Society of New
York, to be held in the Astor House
the evening of April 9. The invitation
was presented by a committee of the
officers and members of the society
headed by Hiram Maxim. The Presi-
dent said he had some engagements in
New York about that time and would
accept the invitation if he could find
the time.

The New Jersey State Bankers Asso-
ciation holds its annual meeting at At-
lantic City in May, and a committee
headed by Adrian Lyon of Newark
asked the President to attend. He said
he feared that he could not accept.

James Burton Reynolds of the tariff
board introduced to the President B. J.
Shoninger, president of the American
Chamber of Commerce of Paris, France.
The President was interested in the
statistical information that Mr. Sho-
ninger was able to give him.

Philadelphia, Nov. 4.—In a game that was infinitely harder than the score would seem, the Carlisle Indians this afternoon added further to Pennsylvania football humiliation by defeating the Red and Blue by the score of 16-7. Most of the scoring was done in the first period; all had been made early in the third and during this time the redskins swept the Quakers completely off their feet by the swiftness and the certainty of their attack. Straight football was mingled with clever end running and forward passes, and in every department of the game the warriors of Carlisle showed their superiority. With the lead gained so early in the game and with victory certain, the Indians were content to play more on the defensive during the last half of the game, and though they more than once threatened Penn's goal, their tries for field goals went wide.

Winning the toss, which the big crowd considered a bad omen at the start, the Indians hurled themselves into the fray, and ere before Penn, or her supporters knew what was going on, had scored. Keoush took the kick off on Penn's 5-yard line and advanced the ball ten yards before he was downed. Straight football was out of the question, and Thayer was compelled to punt. Arcasa getting the ball at midfield. Here is where the Indians started running rings around Penn, the speedy halfback by two end runs of fifteen yards each bringing the ball dangerously near the Penn goal. Welth took a turn, and finding Penn's end vulnerable, tore off another fifteen yards while Howell pushed his way through the centre for five more. Then, with the ball inside the Quaker 10-yard line, Lone Star skirted Penn's weak left end for the first touchdown, to which McWashe added the extra point.

That score, so soon after play started, took much of the fight out of the Quakers, and it was no surprise when, few minutes later, after an exchange of punts, that Welth, getting the ball on the Indians' 15-yard line on a punt, and aided by clever interference, threaded his way through the entire Red and Blue team for the second touchdown. It was a most spectacular run, only made possible by the compact and splendid interference of almost the entire Indian team.

Penn had not recovered from her surprise when the team had changed ends, and though she succeeded in fighting the tactics, the Indians were carrying the play right to the Red and Blue who on every occasion kicked whenever danger threatened.

The play was hard and fierce, and, elated on by the wild entreaties of her cohorts, Penn played desperate football. The Indians retaliated, and there was a mix-up in which Roberts was ruled off for slugging, but Large, who took the vacated place at end, played a brilliant game, and Penn was unable to make any gains around his side of the line. The third period had barely begun when it was seen that Penn had changed her tactics by the frequency with which she used the forward pass and attempted to skirt the ends. But the forward passes were badly handled, and, recovering one of these on the Quakers' 15-yard line, Powell in two plays carried it by straight football to Penn's 2-yard line, and the resultant touchdown by Arcasa was easy. Once again before this period was up the Indians had the ball dangerously near Penn's goal, but the Quakers strenued and a field goal was tried that narrowly missed the bar.

There was no more scoring after this, and the battle was mostly fought out in midfield. Both teams tried to gain by open play, but the results were infinitesimal so that when the whistle blew the ball was near the centre of the field. In those closing moments the Penn. coaches rushed fresh material into the line and backfield in order to at least save the humiliation of shut-out, but the crafty Indians played the game safely, and with victory in their grasp successfully played out time. The Indian team, as a whole was a galaxy of stars, in which Welth, Arcasa, Burd, McWashe and Lone Star scintillated. The teamwork of the Indians was the best seen on Franklin Field this fall, and there never was a moment when the man with the ball was left unprotected. The interference of the Indians was quick in forming and protected the runner so well that many of the Quaker tackles were vain. Nowhere was this seen to better advantage than in Welth's clever run almost the length of the field in the first period. Fast as a streak the Indians showed wonderful power in straight football, but their end running was a revelation.

For Pennsylvania, Thayer, Minds and Dillon played well, but the weakness of Penn's ends had much to do with the Indians' big score.

Where the man and woman are fairly mated, and there is genuine love between them, there is no hardship for either in this arrangement, and usually their condition betters with their years.


But there is a species of man who will lie to his wife about his income; who will sacrifice her twelve months in the year to make it possible for him to be "a sport" and to spend his money where it pleases him to spend; and it is this stripe of man who is running the divorce statistics of the U. S. to the world's limit.


If there is anything on earth more calculated to drive the average woman to despair than having to ask her husband for money, the Recording Angel hasn't given it a prominent place in his Book. And yet, nine tenths of the middle class men will hold to their pocketbooks like a baby to its milk-bottle, and howl just as loud as the baby, if separated from it.


There's just one favor some women ask of Fate, and that is to be the second wife of a man whose wife has been one of the patient, toiling, self-sacrificing sort, who stifled every longing, smothered every desire and who could spell the word "economy" backward and in four different languages.


When this sort of man becomes a widower and has to rely on hired help, his second wife need ask no odds of the most pampered daughter of wealth—provided she has a level head and a goodly store of common sense.

G.. B. Stayman an actor appearing
at one of the local theatres played a
new part on Thursday when he spent
an hour in the county Jail Of Kenosha
county pending hearing on charges
of grand larceny and the arrest and
release of the man proved to be one
of the most interesting stories of the
day in Kenosha. Stayman and the
company with which he is connected
had recently played an engagement
at Mishawaka, Indiana, and while in
that city the members of the company
had stopped at the home Of Joseph
Cunningham, we'll known man of the
Indiana city. Last Sunday night af


ter the play actors had left Misha~
waka Cunningham missed three rings
including one diamond ring. The rings
were valued at $50. Cunningham
traced the company to Kenosha and
on Thursday Sheriff Andrew Stahl re-
ceived letter from him asking that
an effort be made to secure the arrest
of Stayman and the recovery of the
property. A few minutes after the
sheriff had received the letter he saw
bunch of people coming up the street
and their appearance caused him to
suspect that they were actors. He de-
cided to take a chance and went out
in front of the jail and halted them.
Stayman was one of the members Of
the party. The trio was taken into
the office Of the Jail and when the
sheriff declared that he was going to
search them Stayman came to the
front and declared that he had the
rings and that search Of the other
members of the party would not be
necessary. Stayman was at once tax
en- into custody but he turned over
the rings without further complaint
Then the wires were got busy between
Mishawaka and Kenosha and Cum
bingham was informed that his prop
erty had been recovered. He declared
that he had no desire to push the
charges against the actor and that he
would be willing to have him dis
charged from custody if the rings were
returned and all costs of the proceed
ings paid. Stayman lost no time in
making up his mind and within an
hour after he had been taken to the
Jail neat express package with the
charges paid was started for Misha-
waka and in addition all the telephone
and telegraph costs were paid. Stay
man was released and appeared as
usual in the evening and no one save
the members of the company knew
that he had escaped standing trial on
charges of grand larceny.

Washington April 3.—The President to-day forestalled the proposed introduction by the Democrats of a resolution upon the Chief Executive for information pertaining to the mobilization of troops on the Mexican border by giving Representative Sulzer, Flood, and Garner of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs all the data he had on the Mexican situation.

Representative Foster discussed with the President the proposed arbitration treaty with Great Britain and, when leaving the White House, predicted a formal arbitration treaty with England, France, and the United States as signatories. The Secretary of State was an early caller and spent some time with the President discussing arbitration. Andrew Carnegie, who is interested in the pursuit of worldwide peace, called at the Executive Office, but did not see the President.

Washington, D. C., December 6.
The administration plan for settlement of the Jewish passport question was presented to Congress to-day in a bill providing for a commission consisting of three Senators, three members of the House and three citizens, to be appointed by the President, the committee to consider all matters pertaining to the problem now vexing President Taft and his Cabinet, and make report to the administration and to Congress.

"I do not think the abrogation of the treaty of 1882 will result in any relief to our citizens who are complaining of bad treatment by Russia," said Mr. Foster. "The trouble, as I understand it, lies with the Duma although it may be true that the Russian government is behind the Duma in its failure to give proper recognition to the American passports.

"While Russia would not like our abrogation of the treaty, such abrogation of itself as I am informed, will not close the ports of entry of Russia or of the United States against the commerce and citizens of the respective countries; neither will it result in the severance of diplomatic and consular relations. I cannot see where our citizens who are now complaining for justice of their treatment by Russia will be benefited.

"It is my idea that a commission should be appointed and sent to Russia to study all the matters involved, the passport and diplomatic differences between this government and Russia, and recommend appropriate action by this government. I anticipate that good will come of such visit through the meeting of our commissioners with the diplomatic officers of Russia, and the leaders of the Duma, and that without any action by this government the Russian leaders may find a way to modify their regulations so that exact and equal justice under present privilege shall be granted.

"I want it understood that my resolution for a commission is not presented to the House at the request of the State Department, or at the suggestion of Secretary Knox, but because I think it gives the best chance for an early and amicable settlement of differences between the two countries and because I do not think the abrogation of the treaty of 1882 will accomplish this end."

STAUNTON, VIRGINIA

Perfect Weather Conditions Help

to Make Occasion Notable One

With weather conditions which could hardly have been more favorable had they been made to order, Monday's Labor Day celebration held under the auspices of the Working Men's Fraternal Association was the greatest and grandest ever. From first to last it was a big success; from the parade in the morning until the band played "Dixie" in the concert given at the park at night, the occasion was thoroughly enjoyed by the Staunton people and their several thousand guests.

Tremendous Crowd.

They were all here. Vivian and Percy showed up almost with the sun, she in her prettiest dress, and he in his new fall suit. With them came pa and ma and the baby and pretty much everybody else within a radius of good many miles. As early as 8 o'clock a great throng filled the streets, and when an hour and a half later the word was passed that the procession was on the move, the crowd was so dense in Main street that it overflowed the sidewalks.

The hands on the town clock said half past ten when the great line which had been forming in North Central Avenue for two hours moved west on Frederick street to Jefferson. It was exactly three minutes to 11 when the Stonewall Brigade Band swung down Main street and passed the Y. M. C. A. corner.

Following the band, the mounted police and the chief marshal of parade, Frank B. Yount, came the military, Staunton's two crack companies, the Rifles, under command of Captain H. L. Opie, and the West Augusta Guards, captain, Hampton Wayt. Always popular with the people, the soldiers got in extra loud hand Monday as they rode through the streets with the procession of seasoned troopers.

Officials in Line.

Next in line came an open hack with Mayor Wayt, Judge Henry W. Holt, of the Corporation Court, Captain William H. Kable, of the Board of Aldermen, and Police Justice Joseph H. Glasgow. After the officials came the popular Roman Cornet band, spick and span in neat blue uniforms, and playing corking good music. A new feature of the parade this year was the Boy Scouts, that juvenile organization which has come into existence here within recent months. Clad in their khaki uniforms, and marching with the precision of the soldiers in front of them, the little fellows made the best kind of showing. Following the boys were the Patriarchs Militant whose handsome uniforms won them the admiration of the crowd.

Firemen in Line.

Firemen from Staunton, Lexington and Clifton Forge came next, the visitors in neat uniforms which gave them most attractive appearance, locals in their flaming red shirts, which compelled attention even when the line was still four blocks away. Many a Staunton person who stood in the crowd as they passed by recalled one wild night in March when the Clifton Forge men made record run over the mountains to our assistance, and let it be known that that night has not been forgotten by the people.

Besides those already mentioned, there were two other good bands in line, both of which made splendid music. As is always the case, this was one of the most attractive features of the day, and the several different visiting bands were given recognition no less cordial or appreciative than was given our own musicians.

It would be a difficult attempt to mention every one and all the concerns represented in the procession. It would be a task almost as daunting as would be involved in making a complete list of Labor Day visitors. Many blocks one gayly decorated float followed another, the whole lining to form a most attractive spectacle. Practically every town of Industry was represented, for some of the floats showed strikingly in their get-up. The mass of the parade was more than dazzling, and reflected great credit upon the firms who entered into it. Carrying stalks of regulation corn of county height, members of the Corn Club got a big reception ton as they passed in line. It was a feature especially of the day.

Washington, D. C. Dec. 8.—Imprisonment in the penitentiary as punishment of bank officials who accept a commission or other personal compensation on loans made by their bank is recommended by Lawrence O. Murray, comptroller of the currency, in his annual report to congress, published today.

The dishonest practice by officers of national banks of receiving personal compensation for loans made by the bank is a growing evil and has already reached such proportions as to call for criminal legislation on the subject," says the comptroller.

In this manner either the bank is defrauded of lawful interest which it would otherwise receive, or usurious interest is exacted of a borrower by a corrupt officer. A secret reward to the officers is sometimes a deliberate bribe for obtaining loan on insufficient security."

Mr. Murray urges new laws for the punishment of the offense.

The report shows that the banking business of the United States made a substantial growth in the past year, though the gains made were not up to the average annual increases of the past ten years.

The aggregate amount of assets of the national banks increased during the year approximately $3,500,000, or 5.63 per cent. Loans and discounts increased only 1.85 per cent in the face of an average 10-year increase of 6.52 per cent. Individual deposits, representing 80 per cent of bank liabilities, reached the highest point in history, September 30, 1910. This high record, however, was an increase of only 3.50 per cent over the previous year, as compared with a 10-year average increase of 7.49 per cent.

Banking Power 21 Billion.

The net earnings of the national banks during the fiscal year ended June 30 last were $156,985,513, from which dividends were paid to the amount of $114,685,411 or 5.64 per cent on the capital, and 6.53 per cent on the combined capital and surplus.

Only three national banks were placed in the hands of receivers during the year ending October 31.

Greatest stock of Gold And Silver.

Indianapolis, Ind., Dec. 15.--Government officials, aiding in conducting the investigation of the dynamit conspiracy before the federal grand jury, today learned details of explosions in which it is said others than the McNamuras were implicated.

W. E. Griffin, chief of police of Kansas City, Mo., who has knowledge of five explosions in Kansas City, was questioned about certain facts which it is said have never been revealed. As not more than two of these explosions were confessedly the work of Ortie McGranal, Griffin's information was sifted as to who else might have destroyed the property.

Much important testimony bearing on the records taken from the headquarters of the International Association of Bridge and Structural Iron Workers was also obtained from Miss Mary Dye. Until several years ago, Miss Dye, now of Pittsburg, was confidential secretary in the iron workers headquarters. Mrs. Andrew J. Hull, the iron workers' former bookkeeper, also visited the federal building.

Many hotel clerks from various parts of the country have been subpoenaed to tell what they know of the movements of McGranal.

It was intimated that the iron workers' officials were not opposing the government's efforts to expose all implicated in the dynamiting. About thirty thousand papers are to be digested for the benefit of the grand jury.

Burns After comments.

Cleveland, O., Dec. 15.--Declaring other arrests in the McNamara case may be expected and that attempts to buy him and his men had been made, Detective W. J. Burns made an address here today before 100 members of the National Metal Trades Association. Burns made another attack on Samuel Gompers, president of the American Federation of Labor, declaring that he would not cease his attacks until Gompers is thrown out of organized labor.

He also denounced what he called the "corrupt political crowd that controls organized labor."

"There are many McNamaras in organized labor," he said.

Burns said that after concluding his work at Indianapolis he will go to Los Angeles and also that he proposed claiming the rewards offered by various persons or organizations for the arrest and conviction of those guilty of the Los Angeles Times explosion. In 1898 Schwarzschild and Sulzberger entered the combination, the witness said.

He testified that a record was kept of the amount of meat shipped to the different branches and weekly statements were sent to members showing the cost, average price received and the margin of profit on fresh beef in the different cities.

April 2—The undertaking, started in Worcester County twenty-eight months ago, to bring about conquest of tuberculosis among wage earners through an agreement among merchants and manufacturers to provide curative treatment, has had such convincing results according to Dr. Melvin G. Overlook, State Medical Inspector for the Worcester district, that the movement has now extended throughout New England, has crossed the boundary line into New York, going as far west as Ohio, and has given rise to experiments in Japan and Bulgaria, and inquiries from Great Britain, France and elsewhere. gotten to the sufferers across the

Chapel Hill, N. C., June 24.-With the admirable address of Governor W. Kitchin, which was replete with genial humor and sound, wholesome advice, the special public lectures of the third week of the University summer school for teachers were brought to a close on Friday night.

Recognizing the teacher as the means through which our civilization is to be advanced, and by which the foundation of our happiness is laid, Governor Kitchin voiced the sentiments of the high-minded teacher when he said: I want to see this State so grounded in the fundamental virtues and in universal intelligence that our farmers would never know want, and would never serve any cause except the cause of Justice, and our manufacturers and our bankers, our merchants and our physicians, and all our citizens in every walk of life would be as high-minded, as unselfish, as progressive, as thoroughly honest as the highest Greek was in the days of Pericles.

To this end, he said, upon the duty of increasing the pupils' intelligence in order that he may move with freedom among an intelligent citizenry, of impressing upon the child the necessity of being honest, whatever else he may be, and of teaching the youth to be courageous in the presence of untoward circumstances and real danger.

Quoting from the poem, "A Man Dwells Beside the Road," Governor Kitchin beautifully illustrated the value of cultivating in the children of the State the faculty of being friendly. If you do any good in this world, he said, you have got to do it through your friends, illustrating his point by an anecdote of a farmer in Caswell County. The Caswell County man had been buying wagons and buggies for years from a dealer. Upon a purchase he discovered that he had paid his friend a good round profit of about twenty-five dollars. When met in Danville he demonstrated with the dealer because he had made so much profit out of him, and, that too, when they were special friends. The dealer looked him in the eye a moment and said, See here, John, did you know that it is only through my friends I make my profits. I can't sell a single thing to my enemies. They won't buy from me.

vast, impenetrable blue wall, sweep.
ing toward us upon the run. Where but
a brief moment before the plain ap.
peared deserted, it was now fairly
alive with soldiery, the sun gleaming
on fixed bayonets, and faces aglow
with the ardor of surprise. Someone
had blundered! The thin, unsup
ported line of gray infantry directly
in our front closed up their shattered
ranks hastily in desperate effort to
stay the rush. We could see them jam.
ming their muskets for volley fire,
and then, with clash and clatter that
drowned all other sounds, a battery of
six black guns came flying madly past
us, every horse on the run, dashed
into frenzy by his wild rider. With
carriage and caisson leaping at every
jump, the half-naked, smoke-begrimed
cannoneers clinging to their seats like
monkeys, they dashed recklessly for.
ward, swung about into position, and
almost before the muzzles had been
well pointed, were hurling canister
into that blue, victorious advance.
How those gallant fellows worked!!
their guns leaping into air at each
discharge, their movements like clock.
work! Tense, eager, expectant, every
hand among us hard gripped on sabre;
we could not be delayed, while from
end to end, down the full length of
our straining line, rang out the yell
of exultant pride.


"STEADY, men; steady there, lads!"
called the old Colonel, sternly, his old
eyes filled with tears. "Our turn will
come."


Torn, rent, shattered, bleeding,
treading upon the dead and mangled
in rows, those iron men in blue came
on. They were as demons laughing at
death. No rain of lead, no hail of
canister, no certainty of destruction
could check now the fierce impetus
of that forward rush. God knows it
was magnificent; the supreme effort
of men intoxicated with the enthusi.
asm of war! Even where we were,
we could see and feel the giant power
in those grim ranks of steel—the tat.

deep-toned chorus of "GLORY, glory,
hallelujah," that echoed to their tread.

The manufacturers of plug tobacco have been large consumers of wood for many years. Owing to the tendency of tobacco to absorb taste and stain from wood when brought in contact with it in the box, much difficulty has often been met in procuring suitable box material. The mill men furnished the cypress lumber for the tests, and the tobacco manufacturers made the boxes, filled them with tobacco and subjected it to conditions that would bring out any unsuitable properties the wood might have.

Summary of results shows that plug tobacco kept four months in cypress boxes remained sound and in good condition and absorbed no taste from the wood. The box itself is not considered quite as handsome as sycamore, but is lighter in weight, an item worth considering when large shipments are made. The chief economic advantage, however, consists in finding plentiful material for boxes which will meet the needs of the packers and at the same time providing a market for a class of lumber which heretofore has been in small demand.

In the general opinion of those at the ringside neither white hope showed any advancement Wednesday night toward their aspirations of some day wrestling the world's championship from Jack Johnson. The heavier Oklahoma man, weighing 225 pounds, as compared with Kennedy's 215, was considered too slow, and Kennedy's much praised foot work proved a disappointment.

The New York man showed great gameness in taking punishment. He had so much of the worst of it in the latter rounds that many of the spectators shouted to Referee Dan Tom to stop the bout, but he declined to interfere.

The first round was even, with Morris' best blows, lefts and rights to the body and Kennedy's left jabs to the face. Morris rushed in in the second with left to the face, followed by lefts and rights to the head and stomach. Kennedy sent back a couple of left jabs to the face.

Morris kept forcing through the third round with rights and lefts to the body and a left to the face. Kennedy also got in swinging left to the Westerner's face and followed with a right swing to the jaw. They exchanged body blows and were in the midst of a hot rally when the bell rang. It was Morris' round.

Morris was the aggressor again in the fourth but in the end honors went to Kennedy. After taking a right and left to the head and being forced into neutral corner, Kennedy exchanged left blows with Morris and got a bleeding nose. Kennedy came back, however, with a shot of his right to the jaw, staggering Morris to the ropes at the end of the round.

Morris in the sixth punched Kennedy severely by short arm jolts, left upper cuts and a straight left on Kennedy's nose, which made it bleed the more. From this on Morris was all over his man, with Kennedy fighting back as gamely as he could. The bout ended with a rally in which both were doing infighting. They clinched several times and in the breaks, aways Morris got in the more telling blows.

The only damage Morris showed was swelling of his lips while Kennedy was bleeding profusely at the nose and was severely battered.

There are few persons in the United States more interesting than James II. Jones, the negro who served throughout the Civil War as bodyguard and personal servant to Jefferson Davis, president of the Confederate States of America. Probably there is no man who has adhered with greater tenacity to a promise than this aged man, who time after time has refused to disclose the secret of where he hid the great Confederate seal, just before Richmond was evacuated, although museums, patriotic societies and public-spirited individuals have offered him small fortunes for his knowledge.

Made to take a solemn oath by President Davis that he would hide the seal in some spot where it could not be found, and never disclose its whereabouts, the negro has been true to his trust and he declares that there is not enough money in this world to tempt him to break his trust with Mr. Davis. Jones, who is a part Cherokee Indian, is a stanch Confederate, probably for no other reason than Jefferson Davis was the head of the cause, regarded highly by his employer, honored by Mrs. Davis and treated as a friend by the children of President Davis, all of whom, with one exception, he has carried to their last resting place in the family plot in Richmond. The suggestion that he give, or sell, the secret, brings tears of righteous indignation into the old man's eyes. Bent almost double with age, and barely able to walk from one end of the room to the other, and well nigh penniless, he, however, had his reward for his loyalty in the friendship of the most prominent Southerners in the United States Senate today.

Through the influence of these friends he was appointed to the stationery room in the Senate wing of the Capitol, and although his health has prevented him from attending to his duties for over two years, he has been allowed indefinite sick leave on full salary.

Jones was born a free negro more than 50 years ago. His childhood was spent in the town of his birth, Raleigh, N. C., where he lived until the death of his father, James II. Jones. Then leaving his mother, who was almost pure-blooded Cherokee Indian, he started out to earn his own living.

While working in the old St. Charles Hotel, in New Orleans, in 1859 Jefferson Davis took a liking to him and engaged him as personal servant and bodyguard. From the first day of his employment Mr. Davis imposed the utmost confidence in his valet, and though Jones had been called a trusty servant by many of his former employers he never enjoyed quite as much confidence as that which Davis placed in him. It was this which brought about, he says, his great faithfulness to the Confederate leader.

From the moment that the first gun of the Civil War was fired at Fort Sumter until he was released from Fort Monroe, where he had been imprisoned with his employer, Jones never left his employer, except on the one occasion, shortly before the fall of Richmond, when Mr. Davis sent him with Mrs. Davis and the children, together with about $13,000, to Charlotte, N. C. After taking Mrs. Davis and the children there, he hauled the money around in a freight car, he says, from place to place, through the South until he was relieved of his charge by Capt. Parker, near Washington, Ga.

After he had been relieved of his charge in Washington, Ga., he returned with all haste to Richmond where he helped President Davis prepare for the last flight. They fled from the fallen Confederate capital together, generally travelling by night. Mr. Davis and his servant encamped on the night of May 8, 1865, not far from Irwinville, Ga. The next morning when breaking camp, Jones packed Mr. Davis' cane, which Mr. Davis was going to abandon, though he carried it all through the war. When they were captured in Irwinville, May 10, Jones managed to keep the cane and carried it with him to Fort Monroe, where both were imprisoned.

of affairs, and would put a considerable burden of expense upon the
party or upon individuals.


For ourselves, we are not confident that this so-called primary law,
either for the selection of delegates or for senatorial candidates,
will prove a panacea for all political
ills. The man who has money
enough to organize every precinct
in the state is likely to be, as
Stephenson was in Wisconsin, the
leader in the senatorial race. The
primary is quite likely to aid the
man of wealth, or the good fellow
who can kiss all the babies in
the county—and it does not necessarily follow that the best nominee
for the office is the man whom the
people choose.


We have in Colorado Springs
the primary method of selecting
our city commissioners and we have
not yet heard of anybody pointing
with pride to the results of that
system.


But we are to try it in this state
next year and we shall all be better able to judge by its actual results on a large scale than we are.
Springs Telegraph.

Cheraw, Dec. 30.—Judge Watts to-day heard returns to his restraining order of a week ago. Two actions were heard as one.

The town pleading to restrain the Seaboard from obstructing its streets and Coast Line to be allowed to use its right of way, to be left in possession of its property and not to be interfered with in laying the crossing.

Arguments were made for the Seaboard by Messrs. Lyles and Stevenson, and the Coast Line by Messrs. Wilcox and Pollock.

Judge Watts made the following orders:

Order in case of Coast Line against Seaboard Air Line: On hearing pleadings, return and other affidavits herein on rule to show cause why injunction should not be granted and after argument of counsel, and it appearing that the plaintiff obtained an order from the resident Circuit Judge and condemned the crossing referred to in the pleading herein, according to law, and obtained the consent of the railroad commissioners of the State on two separate occasions, that the defendant attempted to obtain an injunction and restraining order from his Honor, Judge Devore, presiding in this circuit, which was refused; that they appealed from this order to the Supreme Court and applied for an order there staying all proceedings until the appeal could be heard, which was refused.

It appears to me that I have no authority to review these orders and that plaintiffs are entitled to put in the crossing under the terms and conditions as allowed by the railroad commission. It is, therefore, ordered, decreed and adjudged that the temporary restraining order granted herein be continued until the final hearing of the case herein, and that plaintiffs enter into bond in the sum of two hundred and fifty dollars before and to be approved by the clerk of Court of the county within ten days, with surety, the said bond to be the usual injunction bond; that the plaintiff be allowed to put in its crossing over the right of way, sidings, tracks and main line of said railroad, in accordance with permission and instructions of the railroad commission allowing the same; that the defendant, its agents, employees and servants be enjoined and restrained from any manner interfering with the plaintiffs in doing the same. It further appearing to my satisfaction that there has been considerable agitation, bad blood and excitement over this matter between the parties to this suit, it is ordered that J. P. Douglass, sheriff of Chesterfield County, see that this order is executed and enforced.

(Signed) X. G. Watts, Dec. 30, 1910, Judge.

In the case of the town of Cheraw, plaintiff against the Seaboard Air Line Railroad: On hearing return rule to show cause why injunction should not issue in the above case, and after argument of counsel, it is ordered that the defendant, its agents and servants be enjoined and restrained until final hearing of cases upon its merits from in any manner obstructing or interfering with the streets described in the pleadings herein, except as double track provided for in the deed of plaintiff to Palmetto Railroad, in 1856. Let the plaintiff enter into the usual injunction bond to be approved by the clerk of Court of this county, in the sum of two hundred and fifty dollars within ten days from this date, Dec. 30.

(Signed) X. G. Watts, Judge 4th Circuit.
